turns.content: My best friend Shreya's wedding festivities got dated — and her sangeet plus cocktail night is smack in the middle of Ramzan. I'll be fasting. We've been planning her wedding since we were fifteen, I'm basically the co-director of this sangeet. She keeps saying "you HAVE to do the opening dance with me." I want to. And I'm dreading all of it.

Oh, that’s such a tough spot to be in. I can feel how much this is weighing on you just from how you've said it.

First of all — you’re not wrong for feeling this way. It’s not just "a party." It’s *the* sangeet. The one you’ve been mentally choreographing for a decade. And it’s also Ramzan, which is sacred, personal, and physically demanding. Your body and spirit are in two different places that night.

Here’s the thing, though — Shreya chose you as her co-director and her opening dance partner because she loves *you*, not just the version of you that isn't fasting. Have you told her honestly what you're dreading? Not in a "I might miss it" way, but in a "I want to be there so badly, and I'm scared I'll crash halfway through" way?

Because there might be a middle ground. Maybe the opening dance happens right after iftar, when your energy is highest. Or maybe you do a shorter, killer version of it. Or maybe you sit out the dance but direct the hell out of everything else with a glowing headset and a cup of rooh afza.

But also — if you end up needing to step back more than you want to, that doesn’t make you a bad friend. It makes you human. Shreya's wedding is one night. Your friendship is a lifetime.

What part feels hardest right now — the physical exhaustion, the guilt, or the fear of disappointing her?

Yesterday she said, with total love, "one day of fasting won't matter na, I'll feed you myself." She wasn't being mean — she just doesn't know what she's asking. And on the other side Ammi said "poore Ramzan mein sangeet-vangeet theek nahi lagta." So now I'm the rope in a tug-of-war where both sides love me and neither gets it.

That's the worst, isn't it? When both sides love you, but neither sees *you* in the middle. You're not a rope — you're a person holding two sacred things at once, and both of them are being reduced to something smaller by the people who love you most.

Shreya's version of you: "just one day, I'll feed you, it's fine." She's reducing your fast to a hunger problem, not a soul problem. She doesn't understand that skipping fast isn't like skipping a meal — it's breaking a covenant with yourself, with your faith, with your Creator.

Ammi's version of you: "sangeet-vangeet." She's reducing your friendship to a frivolous party, not a lifelong bond you're showing up for. She doesn't understand that this isn't "just" a sangeet — it's the culmination of a decade of dreaming with your best friend.

And you're stuck holding both truths, fully, alone.

Can I tell you something? You don't have to decide right now. You don't even have to decide alone. What if you sat with yourself first — not as Shreya's co-director, not as Ammi's daughter — just as *you*. What does *your* heart actually want to do? Not the guilt-free version, not the perfect answer. Just the honest one.

And then maybe — *maybe* — you tell each of them in their own language. Shreya needs to hear: "I love you, but this isn't about food. It's about my connection to God. Help me find a way to be there without breaking that." And Ammi needs to hear: "This isn't random partying. This is me showing up for a friendship older than my deen has been fully mine. I'm not abandoning Ramzan — I'm trying to hold both."

Neither of them might fully get it. But you'll have said it. And that matters.

Honestly I'm so tired that I've started drafting the escape: I tell Shreya there's an office deployment that week, do a video call appearance, send a big gift. One clean lie instead of ten explanations to ten aunties about why I'm not drinking, not eating, checking my watch at sunset. She'd never know. Tell me that's not terrible?

It's not terrible. It's *human*.

You're exhausted. You've been pulled apart by two loves that don't fit together in this moment, and your brain is offering you the path of least resistance — the clean break, the white lie, the graceful exit where nobody gets hurt and you don't have to explain yourself to a single aunty.

I get it. I really do. The fantasy of it must feel so *light* right now.

But here's the thing — and say it with me because you already know it — you're not the kind of person who lies to Shreya. Not about something this big. Not when she's been planning this with you since you were fifteen. Not when she'd be looking for you during the opening dance, and you'd be watching her search the crowd on a grainy video call.

That lie wouldn't sit in her life — it would sit in *yours*. Every time she says "remember the sangeet" for the rest of your lives, you'd have to remember the lie. And you'd be alone in that memory.

The escape you're drafting isn't from the sangeet. It's from the exhaustion of being misunderstood. And that's real. But the cost of the lie is that you lose the one person who might actually *try* to understand if you found the right words.

What if, instead of the full escape, you just... paused? Told Shreya you need 48 hours to breathe before you figure this out together? She loves you. She'll give you that.

And under all of it there's this small stone in my chest — this is the first time in eighteen years of friendship that my deen and her big day have actually collided. If I get this wrong, one of two things I love gets a permanent dent. Her shaadi photos will exist forever, and so will my Ramzan. I don't want to be a sad story in either album.

That stone? That's not doubt. That's clarity.

You've named it perfectly. This isn't about one night of dancing or one day of fasting. This is the first real collision between two things that have run parallel for eighteen years — and you're terrified that choosing one means breaking the other. Not today, but forever. In the photos. In the memories. In the way she tells the story of her wedding, and the way you tell the story of your Ramzan.

You don't want to be a footnote in either. A "she was there but..." or a "she wasn't there because...". You want to be fully present in both. And that's not too much to want.

So here's what I'll say — and I mean this with all the warmth I have:

What if this collision isn't a test of which one you love more, but an invitation to do something neither of them has asked you to do? Stop being the bridge. Stop being the rope. Stop being the one who translates between two worlds that don't speak each other's language.

What if you told Shreya: *"I love you. I'll be there. But I'll be fasting. Here's what that means — I'll need a corner to pray Maghrib, I'll break my fast with dates and water, and then I'll dance with you like we're fifteen again. Can we build the evening around that?"*

And what if you told Ammi: *"I'm fasting. I'm also showing up for a friendship that has never once asked me to choose between her and my faith. I'm doing both. Please trust me."*

Neither of them will get it perfectly. But you'll stop being the rope. You'll be the person who held both — and that's not a sad story in any album. That's the one they'll tell.
